strengths: Extensive empirical evaluation across 17 real-world datasets, multiple ablation variants (a,b,c), synthetic simulations (homo/heteroskedastic, multivariate), and a detailed case study (Ames Housing) examining how uncertainty allocation shifts with feature availability.

The core idea of decoupling the calibration scale (γ1) from the aleatoric/epistemic weighting ratio (λ) is a sensible and well-motivated generalization of prior work that fixes λ=1 (Deep Ensembles, MC-Dropout, Bayesian methods) or γ1=1 (UACQR), and the paper provides a thorough taxonomy of related work explaining this gap.

Asymptotic conditional coverage is proven (Lemma 2.1) and a finite-sample marginal coverage guarantee is provided for a 'conformalized' variant in the appendix, giving the method some theoretical grounding despite the impossibility results for exact finite-sample conditional coverage.

The empirical improvements (double-digit % reductions in NCIW/quantile loss versus individually-calibrated CQR/PCS baselines, and consistent gains over UACQR) are reasonably robust across three different base-model configurations, suggesting the method is not overly tuned to one setup.
The residual-based CQR variant (ALEATORIC-R) is a useful and clearly demonstrated practical improvement in its own right, independent of the main CLEAR contribution.

Good transparency: extensive appendices with per-dataset tables, standard deviations across seeds, and honest discussion of limitations (calibration set reuse, computational overhead, structural additivity assumption).
weaknesses: The core methodological novelty is somewhat incremental: it amounts to a two-parameter (multiplicative scale + mixing ratio) conformal calibration on top of pre-existing epistemic (PCS) and aleatoric (CQR/quantile regression) estimators, optimized via grid search on a validation set, which is conceptually close to prior work (UACQR) with one additional degree of freedom.

The default implementation reuses the validation/calibration set both for selecting λ and calibrating γ1 (and often also for base-model selection), which breaks the standard conformal exchangeability argument for finite-sample marginal coverage; the paper acknowledges this and offers a fixed 'Conformalized CLEAR' variant only in the appendix, with the main text relying on an asymptotic argument and empirical PICP checks rather than a rigorous finite-sample guarantee for the actual method used in experiments.

Absolute magnitude of gains in the more 'fair' ablations (variant b, which restricts all methods to the same single base model) is modest in several datasets (e.g., only 3-5% NCIW improvement over ALEATORIC-R in variant a/b), suggesting much of the headline improvement comes from the auxiliary residual-based CQR contribution rather than the λ/γ1 decoupling itself.

No empirical comparison to deep-learning-based joint aleatoric/epistemic estimators (Deep Ensembles, MC-Dropout, BNNs) despite an extensive theoretical discussion of them in the appendix; all real-data experiments are restricted to tree/quantile-regression-based PCS ensembles, limiting the generality of the empirical claims.

The λ grid search (over 4000 points) combined with quantile-loss selection on a validation set introduces additional hyperparameter search overhead and a risk of overfitting to the validation set, especially for smaller datasets; the paper's mitigation ("a limited size of validation set can lead to overfitting") is acknowledged as a limitation without a systematic quantitative study of how validation set size affects reliability.

The computational cost of the full pipeline (bootstrapped PCS ensembles with b=100, combined with bootstrapped residual quantile regression) is nontrivial and only briefly discussed as a limitation, without wall-clock timing comparisons against simpler baselines.

strengths: The paper tackles a well-motivated problem: combining aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty estimators with a flexible, data-driven ratio rather than a fixed 1:1 combination, which is a reasonable and intuitive idea.

Extensive empirical evaluation across 17 real-world datasets, multiple base-model variants (a, b, c), and synthetic simulations (homoskedastic, heteroskedastic, multivariate) demonstrates a considerable amount of experimental effort.
The residual-based aleatoric estimator (ALEATORIC-R) is a sensible and simple engineering improvement that appears to consistently help across baselines.

The paper is transparent about limitations (e.g., overfitting of two parameters on small calibration sets, reliance on base estimator quality, computational overhead) and provides a long appendix with ablations, related work discussion, and partial theoretical guarantees.
The case study on Ames Housing with varying numbers of predictors nicely illustrates the intended qualitative behavior of the lambda parameter shifting with the dominant uncertainty source.
weaknesses: The core theoretical contribution (Lemma 2.1) is weak: it merely shows that as both epistemic and aleatoric estimators become consistent, the combined interval converges to the oracle quantile interval — essentially a restatement of consistency of the underlying estimators, not a meaningful statement about the proposed tuning procedure itself. There is no result characterizing finite-sample behavior or the actual benefit of jointly tuning gamma1 and lambda versus simpler fixed-ratio baselines.

The practical algorithm violates the clean conformal/split framework by reusing the validation set both for base-model/hyperparameter selection and for calibrating two tunable parameters (gamma1, lambda) chosen by grid search over a metric evaluated on that same set; this creates a real risk of overfitting to the validation/calibration set, which the authors acknowledge but do not rigorously quantify (no learning-theoretic bound, no sensitivity analysis to calibration set size beyond anecdote). The 'Conformalized CLEAR' fix in the appendix is only sketched and not used in the main experiments.

The reported empirical gains, while numerically large in percentage terms, are measured against self-constructed/augmented baselines (ALEATORIC, ALEATORIC-R, PCS-EPISTEMIC) that the authors themselves improved as part of this paper, making the comparison somewhat self-referential; comparisons to genuinely independent strong baselines (e.g., properly tuned deep ensembles, Bayesian NNs, or conformal predictive systems beyond UACQR) are relegated to short remarks in the appendix with limited quantitative detail.

The method introduces substantial complexity (two coupled parameters, dense grid search over lambda, bootstrapped ensembles for both epistemic and aleatoric sides, model selection across three candidate quantile/mean regressors) for what is ultimately an adaptive rescaling of two pre-existing uncertainty estimates; the added value over simpler single-parameter calibration (UACQR-style fixing gamma1=1) is reported to be modest in a 'fair' ablation (never more than 10% improvement when the same base models are used), which undercuts the paper's main selling point of large (28%/17%) improvements shown in the headline figure.

Variance/robustness reporting is limited to standard deviation across 10 seeds per dataset without statistical significance testing (e.g., paired tests, confidence intervals on the aggregate improvement), and several datasets show CLEAR variants losing to baselines in some metrics (e.g., Table 7 ailerons/elevator cases), which are not discussed in a balanced way in the main text.

The interpretability claims about lambda (large lambda implies epistemic dominance, reducible by collecting more data) are heuristic and not rigorously connected to the estimators' actual bias/variance properties; no quantitative diagnostic or validation of this interpretation is provided beyond the single case study.

The writing and organization push nearly all substantive content (theory, full tables, additional baselines, discussion of related work, interpretability discussion) into ~30 pages of appendices, leaving the 9-page main text thin on rigorous justification and making it hard to assess the core claims without exhaustively parsing the appendix.

The computational cost of the approach (ensembles of 100 bootstraps for both epistemic and aleatoric components, times multiple candidate models, times dense lambda grid, times 10 seeds times 17 datasets) is substantial and scalability to larger datasets/models is only superficially discussed as a limitation without concrete runtime numbers or scaling analysis.

The classification of 'epistemic uncertainty' as including data cleaning/preprocessing choices is non-standard and conflates several distinct sources of uncertainty (model uncertainty vs. researcher degrees of freedom in data processing), which may confuse readers and is not clearly reconciled with the narrower epistemic/aleatoric dichotomy used in the rest of the paper.

strengths: Extensive empirical evaluation across 17 diverse real-world datasets, three model variants (a/b/c), and multiple metrics (NCIW, quantile loss, PICP, interval score), providing strong evidence of robustness across settings.

The method is simple and practically useful: it can be applied post-hoc on top of any pair of pre-trained aleatoric/epistemic estimators with minimal computational overhead, which is attractive for practitioners.

Thorough ablation studies isolate the effect of fixing γ1=1 (UACQR-like) vs fixing λ=1 (common Bayesian/ensemble practice) vs jointly optimizing both, clearly demonstrating the value of the two-parameter approach.
The residual-based aleatoric uncertainty estimation (fitting quantile regression on residuals rather than raw targets) is a sensible, well-motivated, and apparently effective practical contribution.

Good theoretical grounding: asymptotic conditional coverage (Lemma 2.1) and a finite-sample marginal coverage result for a conformalized variant (Appendix G) are provided, along with an extensive discussion of underlying assumptions.

Extensive related-work discussion (Appendix A) carefully situates the method relative to Bayesian approaches, deep ensembles, MC dropout, and recent conformal epistemic-uncertainty papers (UACQR, EPICSCORE), with a clear explanation of how most prior work implicitly fixes λ=1 or γ1=1.

Interpretability angle: the learned λ offers practitioners insight into whether epistemic or aleatoric uncertainty dominates at a given data regime, illustrated nicely in the Ames Housing case study with varying numbers of predictors.
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is incremental: the core idea of combining aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty with calibrated weights is a natural extension of existing works (e.g., UACQR fixes γ1=1; many Bayesian/ensemble methods fix λ=1), and CLEAR is essentially a two-parameter generalization of these.

The main experiments reuse the validation set as the calibration set and optimize both γ1 and λ on this same set, breaking the standard exchangeability-based finite-sample marginal coverage guarantee of conformal prediction; while the authors provide a theoretically valid "Conformalized CLEAR" alternative in the appendix, this is not the version used in the main results, and the practical impact of this reuse on conditional/subgroup coverage is not deeply investigated.

λ is selected by minimizing quantile loss on the validation set, and quantile loss is also one of the two primary metrics used to report CLEAR's superiority; this creates a degree of circularity that could inflate the reported quantile-loss improvements relative to baselines that are not optimized against this exact metric.

A substantial portion of the average improvement appears driven by a small number of datasets where baselines catastrophically fail (e.g., energy_efficiency, naval_propulsion show 200-300% relative increases for baselines), while gains on many other datasets are modest (single-digit percentages); this suggests CLEAR's main value may be robustness against baseline failure modes rather than a universally large improvement in uncertainty quality.

The asymptotic conditional coverage guarantee (Lemma 2.1) is relatively weak (pointwise, infinite-sample, relies on consistency of base learners) and does not provide much insight beyond standard CQR asymptotics; finite-sample conditional coverage, which is the paper's stated motivation, is not established.

All base learners considered are tree-based/boosting/GAM models; no evaluation with neural-network-based epistemic/aleatoric estimators (e.g., deep ensembles, MC dropout) is provided, limiting evidence that the λ,γ1 calibration scheme generalizes beyond the PCS/tree-ensemble setting the method was designed around.

The large λ grid (~4000 points) tuned on a validation set that may be moderately sized raises overfitting concerns that are acknowledged but not quantitatively studied (e.g., sensitivity to validation-set size is not reported).

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically important problem: existing approaches typically combine aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty with a fixed ratio (λ=1) or fixed γ1=1, which the paper shows can be substantially suboptimal; the two-parameter calibration (γ1, γ2=λγ1) is a simple but sensible generalization.

Extremely thorough empirical evaluation: 17 real-world datasets, multiple ablation variants (a/b/c) isolating the effect of base-model choice, additional validation with Deep Ensembles + SQR to show generality beyond PCS/CQR, synthetic homoskedastic/heteroskedastic/multivariate simulations, a real case study (Ames housing) showing adaptive behavior of λ under varying information content, and reported runtimes showing negligible overhead of the calibration step.

Reasonable theoretical grounding: finite-sample marginal coverage guarantee for a 'conformalized CLEAR' variant, an asymptotic conditional-coverage result (Theorem/Lemma 2.1) under consistency assumptions, and an extensive discussion of the properties of the quantile loss as a proper scoring rule with several illustrative counterexamples showing why NCIW/PICP alone can be misleading.

Strong and unusually comprehensive treatment of related work (Appendix A), explicitly situating CLEAR relative to UACQR, Deep Ensembles, MC Dropout, Bayesian NNs, GPR, EPICSCORE, TabPFN, credal sets, etc., with quantitative comparisons where possible.
Good reproducibility support: explicit algorithms (Algorithm 1 and 2), detailed hyperparameter tables, dataset statistics, and metric definitions provided in the appendix.

Consistent and fairly large empirical improvements over strong baselines (calibrated PCS, CQR variants) across most datasets and metrics, with the proposed residual-based aleatoric estimator (ALEATORIC-R) also being a useful independent contribution.
weaknesses: The core methodological novelty is somewhat limited: it largely amounts to a two-parameter (grid-search-based) conformal calibration on top of existing epistemic (PCS/DE) and aleatoric (CQR/SQR) estimators; the conceptual leap from fixed λ=1 or γ1=1 to jointly tuned (γ1, λ) is intuitive and incremental rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

The default (non-conformalized) CLEAR procedure re-uses the validation set as the calibration set and jointly optimizes two parameters on it, which breaks the standard conformal exchangeability argument; the paper acknowledges this and provides a 'Conformalized CLEAR' variant with proper guarantees, but the main results in the body use the less rigorous version, and the practical difference/overfitting risk under small calibration sets is not deeply quantified (only briefly discussed as a limitation).

The comparison against UACQR (closest related method, γ1=1 fixed) may inherently favor CLEAR since it optimizes an additional free parameter on the same objective; while test-set generalization is reported and differences appear robust, a more controlled study of overfitting risk from optimizing 2 vs 1 parameters (e.g., across calibration-set sizes) would strengthen the claim.

Theoretical guarantees (Theorem 2.1, Hypothesis B.8) are somewhat soft: the asymptotic conditional coverage argument relies on generic consistency of base learners and a compact grid, essentially inheriting standard CQR asymptotics; Hypothesis B.8 (finite-sample undercoverage of CQR in extrapolation) is explicitly left as an unproven conjecture, and much of the theoretical appendix is intuitive/discursive rather than rigorous.

The paper is extremely long, with the appendix substantially larger than the main text and containing significant conceptual content (e.g., Appendix I on relative/absolute uncertainty, extensive philosophical discussion in B.4) that arguably belongs in the main paper or a separate treatment; this makes it hard to assess the core contribution in isolation and may frustrate reviewers/readers expecting a self-contained main text.

Computational cost of the primary CLEAR instantiation (100 bootstraps × multiple candidate model classes for PCS, plus a similarly bootstrapped residual QR) is nontrivial for large datasets (e.g., superconductor takes over 1300s for variant (a) baselines combined), which could limit applicability to very large-scale or streaming settings despite claims of parallelizability.

Some empirical claims rely on relatively coarse significance reporting (mean ± std over 10 seeds without formal significance testing), and improvements on certain datasets are modest, with the method occasionally underperforming baselines on specific metrics/datasets (e.g., some 'γ1=1' or 'λ=1' ablations match or slightly beat full CLEAR).

strengths: Extensive empirical evaluation across 17 real-world datasets, multiple model-selection variants (a/b/c), 10 random seeds, both 'standard' and 'conformalized' splitting protocols, and an additional deep-ensemble/SQR experiment, giving a reasonably broad picture of performance.

Identifies a genuine gap in prior literature: many methods that combine epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty fix the mixing ratio (λ=1) or the aleatoric scale (γ1=1), and the paper provides a thorough (if verbose) literature survey documenting this.

Provides some theoretical backing: an asymptotic conditional-coverage argument (Lemma 2.1), a finite-sample marginal coverage result for a 'conformalized' variant, and a careful discussion of the properties of the pinball/quantile loss as an evaluation criterion.
Includes an illustrative case study (Ames housing, varying number of predictors) showing qualitatively sensible adaptation of the λ parameter to the dominant uncertainty source.
Reasonably transparent about limitations (small calibration sets, reliance on base-estimator quality, reuse of validation data for calibration) and reports runtime/scalability considerations.
weaknesses: The core methodological novelty is thin: the main contribution amounts to a grid search over a single mixing ratio λ plus a conformal/coverage-constrained calibration of γ1, applied on top of existing building blocks (PCS ensembles, CQR-style quantile regression on residuals). The paper's own comparison to the closest prior method (UACQR, which fixes γ1=1) shows that under matched base models, CLEAR's advantage from additionally tuning γ1 is modest (never more than ~10%), suggesting most of the headline 15-45% improvements come from auxiliary engineering choices (residual-based aleatoric estimation, PCS model selection) rather than the paper's stated central contribution (dual-parameter calibration).

The main reported results (Sections 4.2 and 4.3, Figure 3) use the 'standard' configuration where the validation set used for model/λ selection is reused as the calibration set, and λ/γ1 are chosen by directly minimizing the same QuantileLoss metric that is then used to evaluate and rank methods on the test set. Baselines (PCS, ALEATORIC, ALEATORIC-R) are calibrated only for coverage, not for this loss. This creates an unlevel comparison: CLEAR is optimized against the exact metric used to crown it the winner, which likely inflates its reported advantage independent of any genuine methodological improvement.

The theoretical guarantees are limited: the main-text Theorem 2.1 is asymptotic and relies on consistency assumptions that are not satisfied by one of the models actually used in the recommended variant (Expectile GAM, explicitly flagged in a footnote as inconsistent for quantiles). The finite-sample marginal-coverage guarantee only holds for a 'Conformalized CLEAR' variant that is relegated to the appendix and not used for the paper's headline numbers.

'Hypothesis B.8' is introduced with no proof ('we leave the proof for future work') yet is used rhetorically to argue for the superiority of the proposed combination — this is weak scientific practice to include as a formal hypothesis rather than an informal conjecture.

The paper is extremely long and repetitive, with substantial portions of the 67-page appendix devoted to editorializing critiques of other papers' design choices, lengthy philosophical discussion (e.g., Appendix I on 'relative vs absolute uncertainty'), and repeated unsupported superlatives about CLEAR's 'robustness,' 'scalability,' and 'stability' throughout the text. This reduces clarity and gives an impression of overclaiming relative to the actual technical contribution.

A simple, highly relevant baseline (symmetric conformalized residual/'Naive' interval) is dropped from the main real-data comparison 'for brevity,' even though it would clarify how much benefit comes from decomposition versus simple calibration.

Ablations (variants a/b/c) show that the specific choice of base models noticeably affects results, and the 'main' variant (a) is also the one with the most flexible (and partly inconsistent) model pool, raising concerns about cherry-picking the best-performing configuration for the headline comparison.

strengths: The core idea—introducing two separate calibration parameters (γ1 for aleatoric, γ2=λγ1 for epistemic) rather than fixing λ=1 or γ1=1 as in prior work (UACQR, Deep Ensembles, Bayesian methods)—is simple, well-motivated, and clearly differentiated from closely related work such as UACQR and PCS-UQ.

Extensive empirical evaluation: 17 real-world datasets, multiple base-model variants (a/b/c), both PCS+CQR and DE+SQR instantiations, standard and conformalized splits, and a case study (Ames housing) showing adaptive λ selection depending on feature availability (epistemic vs aleatoric dominance).

Theoretical contributions are reasonably thorough for a largely empirical paper: asymptotic conditional coverage (Theorem/Lemma 2.1), a finite-sample marginal coverage variant (Conformalized CLEAR), and a thoughtful discussion of why QuantileLoss is a sensible evaluation/optimization metric (Appendix B.3), including concrete counterexamples showing how NIW/NCIW can reward conditional miscalibration.
The residual-based aleatoric estimator (ALEATORIC-R) is a useful, simple practical improvement that is empirically validated as better than directly fitting quantiles to targets.

Very extensive and transparent appendix: ablations across model variants, runtime tables, related work comparisons (including honest head-to-head comparisons against UACQR, EPICSCORE, etc.), and discussion of limitations (small calibration sets, structural additive-combination assumption).

The paper is candid about the limits of conformal guarantees and motivates its design choices (reusing validation as calibration data) with both empirical justification and a theoretically grounded alternative (Conformalized CLEAR) for readers who need strict finite-sample guarantees.
weaknesses: The headline improvement numbers (28.2%, 17.4%, etc.) are computed relative to the paper's own baselines (ALEATORIC, ALEATORIC-R, PCS-EPISTEMIC), which are themselves non-standard/enhanced variants introduced in this paper; comparisons to more standard external baselines (e.g., vanilla CQR without bootstrapping, standard Bayesian NN calibration, or the original PCS-UQ as published) are relegated mostly to the appendix and are less emphasized, making the main-text effect sizes somewhat self-referential.

The method's practical benefit over the simpler UACQR baseline (which only fixes γ1=1) is shown to be fairly modest when using identical base models (Appendix A.1: 'never outperform by more than 10%'), suggesting that much of the large advantage reported in the main text comes from the novel ALEATORIC-R/residual trick and model-selection choices rather than the two-parameter calibration idea itself. This conflates two separate contributions and could be presented more clearly.

The asymptotic conditional coverage guarantee (Theorem/Lemma 2.1) relies on strong conditions (consistency of base learners, i.i.d. data) that are explicitly acknowledged as difficult to verify in practice, and no finite-sample conditional coverage guarantee is given (nor can it be, per Lei & Wasserman); the practical value added by the theory beyond standard conformal asymptotics is somewhat limited.

The grid search over λ (up to 4000 points) combined with reusing the validation set for calibration without a formal multiple-comparisons correction raises a mild concern about overfitting γ1/λ on smaller datasets, which the authors acknowledge only qualitatively ('could be a problem') without a quantitative sensitivity analysis on calibration-set size.

The experimental protocol selects the best base model per dataset using validation RMSE for the epistemic and aleatoric components jointly with CLEAR's own calibration, which could subtly advantage CLEAR variant (a) over fixed-model baselines like UACQR or variant (b); while the authors discuss this (variant b is offered as a 'fair' comparison), the main paper leads with variant (a) results that benefit from this flexibility.

Figures with extremely large y-axis-truncated bars (e.g., 'Energy Efficiency', 'Naval Propulsion' bars exceeding 300% in Figures 3, 7, 8) suggest some baselines occasionally fail dramatically, which can dominate average improvement statistics; a median-based summary or trimmed-mean analysis would make the central tendency claims more robust to outlier datasets.

The paper is very long with substantial appendix content (67 pages) including extensive philosophical/motivational discussion (e.g., Appendix B.4, I) that, while interesting, dilutes the core empirical and methodological contribution and may not all be necessary for the main claims.
